messages.subject: Re: CODEX log 2 based fold change
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shu,

Apologies for my late reply. You can read in the table in R and get the log ratio of the raw_cov and norm_cov, followed by taking the log transformation. Or if you prefer, you can load your output table into Excel and add a column in Excel which seems to be easier.

Cheers,
Yuchao

Hi Yuchao,

I was following the discussion above with great interest. I wonder whether normalizing all chromosomes together in general has advantages over analyzing each chromosome separately? Althought if I have WES data?

>From the scripts you posted, I saw that you segment on a gene-by-gene basis. This of course saves an annotation step of duplicated/deleted regions afterwards, but does it provide any additional advantages?

Best and thanks a lot for your work!
Jens

Am Montag, 30. März 2015 16:42:46 UTC+2 schrieb Yuchao Jiang:
> Hi Yvan,
>

> 1) Please update your CODEX to 0.99.10.
> 2) Please use the code that I sent you last week to process the entire chromosome altogether (essentially the code extracts read depth, GC content etc from each chromosome separately but does the normalization at one attempt). From the log files you sent me, I believe you ran chr11 and chr12 themselves? This way you only have 24 and 63 targets respectively after QC, which reduces CODEX’s power.
> 3) For your false positive and false negative, usually it’s very hard to define these unless you have gold standard, e.g., paired SNP array calls or array CGH calls. I don’t usually refer to the raw depth coverage matrix (aka, Y matrix) for CNV signals since the data can be noisy and it’s hard to distinguish a CNV signal from artifacts/biases. Nevertheless, targeted sequencing tends to be cleaner than WES and therefore I think your intuition is right. What’s the chosen K by CODEX for your dataset (K=which.max(BIC) by default but the choice of K is not trivial)? I would suggest K=1.
> 4) Finally, do you have case and control samples? If so, please use normalize2() for normalization rather than normalize(). This increases calling accuracy.
> 5) The ’null device’ is from the plotting command — a pdf is generated from your Linux device rather than your “local” device. This isn’t an error.
>
> Let me know if you’ve any questions and please keep me updated on how the new code works on your data! Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: joining the codex group
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jens,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. There are two versions for CODEX. The one we described in our paper and we included in the Bioconductor paper is for whole exome sequencing. It normalizes and segments each chromosome separately. You can combine all chromosomes together for normalization but it's very computationally heavy (n=200,000 exons). For segmentation, naturally and by default we detect CNVs by segmenting each chromosome separately.

We adapt CODEX for targeted sequencing due to general interest. The number of targets are too few if we consider chromosomes separately and thus we normalize all genome-wide targets altogether. For segmentation, we do that on the gene - level as between different genes(targets) the distance can be quite large. So we perform segmentation within each gene.

Hope that this clarifies. Let us know if you have any further questions.

Cheers,
Yuchao

Sent from my iPhone

messages.subject: Re: CODEX for Mus Musculus
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jens,

Apology for my late reply--just got back from a workshop. Attached is the code that I used to generate mappability for human. I am sure you can easily adapt it to the mouse genome. Note that the code has not been optimized and you might need parallel computing to run it efficiently. In CODEX, the mappability is pre-computed and stored for exonic regions.

We will include BSgenome.Mmusculus.UCSC.mm10 as a dependent package and update CODEX to be suited for mouse genome in the next version. Thanks very much for pointing this out.

Cheers,
Yuchao

--
Yuchao Jiang (yuc...@mail.med.upenn.edu)
PhD student in Genomics and Computational Biology
University of Pennsylvania

messages.subject: Re: CODEX for Mus Musculus
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jens,

(1) It’s better if you use your designed targets. What’s done by CODEX by default is that we overlap the input targets with the pre-stored targets whose mappabilities are already calculated. This dramatically reduces the computation time. Also the mappability computation is only for the QC procedure where we remove regions of the genome that are for example, segmental duplication regions.

(2) The script I gave you is only for computing mappability for chr22. The brief idea is that we generate consecutive pseudo-reads covering the exonic regions in chr22 and map them back to the entire genome (note that here it’s not limited to chr22 only as a read might be mapped to multiple different regions in the genome). You will have to run for each chromosome of the mouse. Again, the code isn’t optimized as we didn’t include that in the package however you can run each target from each chromosome in parallel.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao
